scenes.narration: One hundred and twenty-one thousand dollars a year. That is roughly the income you now need to afford the payments on the typical American home.
Five years earlier, it was sixty-eight thousand seven hundred dollars. The houses did not get bigger. They did not get better. The same home simply started to cost a whole extra salary.

keyframes.cue: The houses did not get bigger
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: So how did a house, the most ordinary thing in American life, slip out of reach for so many people?
By the end of this video, you will know the four forces behind it. The price, the loan, the homes that were never built, and the rules that decide what can be built at all.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with a simple yardstick. Take the price of a typical existing home and divide it by the income of a typical household. Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies tracks exactly that. In the nineteen nineties, a home cost about three point two years of income. In twenty nineteen, about four point one. In twenty twenty-five, four point seven times, just below the all-time high of five reached in twenty twenty-two.
The biggest jump came fast. According to the same report, home prices rose fifty-four percent nationwide after twenty twenty. Wages rose too, but nowhere near that fast.

New homes tell the same story over a longer stretch. The Census Bureau's median price for a newly built house sold in the summer of two thousand was one hundred and sixty-eight thousand eight hundred dollars. In the summer of twenty twenty-six, it was three hundred and ninety-three thousand three hundred dollars. These are dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation, but the price more than doubled.

Today, almost five. Every extra block is a whole extra year of work, before taxes, before food, before anything else.

scenes.narration: But almost nobody pays for a house with cash. They borrow. And the price of borrowing changed even faster than the price of the house.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In the first week of twenty twenty-one, the average thirty-year fixed mortgage rate, tracked by Freddie Mac, fell to two point six five percent. That was the lowest point of that period. Then inflation arrived, and interest rates climbed. In early November twenty twenty-six, the same average stood at seven point one eight percent.

Higher prices times higher rates. According to Harvard's housing center, the monthly mortgage payment on the median-priced home reached two thousand four hundred and twenty dollars. At the end of twenty twenty, it was one thousand two hundred and forty dollars. The payment roughly doubled. Add insurance and property taxes, and the total monthly cost of owning that home comes to about three thousand one hundred and twenty dollars.

keyframes.cue: At the end of twenty twenty
keyframes.label: items[0].bars[0].at.cue

scenes.narration: And high rates did something strange. They froze the market. Half of all outstanding mortgages carried rates below four percent at the end of twenty twenty-five. If you sell, you give up that cheap loan and take a new one at around seven. So many owners simply stay put.

The numbers show it. The share of Americans who moved in a year fell to a record low of eleven point two percent in twenty twenty-four. And existing home sales were stuck at four point one million in twenty twenty-five, a thirty-year low, about two thirds of the sales in twenty twenty-one.

Let me draw the lock. Here is an owner with a loan at three percent. Here is the house they would like to move to. Between them, a new loan at seven percent. Moving would mean a much bigger payment for the same kind of home. So the owner stays, the house never comes up for sale, and the buyers waiting outside see fewer homes on the market.

scenes.narration: Rates explain the last few years. But the deeper problem started long before, with the homes that America never built.

keyframes.label: Rates explain the last few years

scenes.narration: Go back to two thousand and eight. The housing bubble burst, builders went bust, and construction collapsed. By our calculation from Census data, about about fifteen and a half million new homes were completed in the two thousands. In the twenty tens, it was about nine million. In twenty eleven alone, completions fell to about five hundred and eighty-five thousand, the lowest year in the Census records, which go back to nineteen sixty-eight.
Meanwhile, the number of households kept growing. Millennials were reaching the age when people buy their first home. Demand rose, and supply did not keep up.

How many homes are missing? Nobody agrees on one number. Harvard's housing center notes that estimates of the shortage range between one point two and five point five million homes. The research group Up for Growth puts the gap at about three point eight million homes. Either way, it is millions of homes that people need and that do not exist.
Builders have picked up the pace again. Completions came back to about one and a half million in twenty twenty-five. But filling a hole that took a decade to dig takes much longer than one good year.

Let me draw the gap. Here is the line of new households, rising steadily year after year. Here is the line of new homes. Before the crash, the two moved together. After the crash, the homes line dropped, and the space between the two lines is the shortage. Too many buyers chasing too few homes means one thing. Higher prices.

scenes.narration: Which raises an obvious question. If homes are so valuable, why not just build more of them? Often, the answer is written in the rules.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In most American cities, local zoning rules decide what can be built on each piece of land. And very often, the answer is one house per lot, and nothing else. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, mapped Greater Los Angeles. They found that about seventy-eight percent of its residential land is reserved for single-family homes only.
That means no apartments, no townhouses, no small duplex, on most of the land where people live. Even where demand is highest, the rules can keep the number of homes fixed.

Then there is the cost of the rules themselves. Permits, fees, codes and delays. The National Association of Home Builders, the builders' own trade group, estimates that regulation makes up about twenty-six point four percent of the price of a new single-family home. On an average new home, that is about one hundred and thirty-two thousand dollars.
That estimate comes from the industry, and many rules protect safety and the environment. But the direction is clear. Every extra step makes a new home slower and more expensive to build.

Let me draw one city block. Here are eight lots. With single-family zoning, each lot gets one house. Eight homes. Now allow small apartment buildings on the same lots. Four homes on each. Thirty-two homes on the same block, with the same streets. The land did not change. Only the rule did.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: High prices, expensive loans, missing homes and tight rules. Put them together, and someone ends up locked outside.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The National Association of Realtors tracks who buys homes. In its latest survey, the typical first-time buyer was forty years old, an all-time high. First-time buyers made up just twenty-two percent of all buyers, about half the historical norm before two thousand and eight.

And there is little on the shelf for them. According to Harvard's housing center, in March twenty nineteen, forty-nine percent of homes listed for sale were affordable to a household earning seventy-five thousand dollars or less. By March twenty twenty-six, it was just twenty-three percent.

The squeeze reaches far beyond the big coastal cities. In twenty twenty, you needed more than one hundred thousand dollars a year to afford the median home in thirty-one metro areas. In twenty twenty-five, it was one hundred and sixty-nine.

Let me put the four forces together. The price, almost five years of income. The loan, at around seven percent. The missing homes, counted in millions. And the rules on the land. Each one pushes the door a little further shut, and the people still outside are the young and the first-time buyers.

scenes.narration: So why did American homes become so expensive? Not because of one villain. A decade of too little building, rules that limit what can be built, and then a jump in prices and rates on top. For owners who bought early, it has been a windfall. For everyone else, the American dream now comes with a much higher price tag.
